why: I compared each check's PASS and FAIL conditions with its expect line. Check 1 asks for argument order (including with the order reversed), the `<file>:<line>: <error>` format, and lines that match the single-file output. All of that comes from "in order" and "as for one file before". Check 2 asks for a `-:1:` prefix, nothing printed for clean stdin, and exit 2 when - is given twice. Check 3 asks for exits 0/1/2/2, an error on stderr, and c still reported after the missing file. Reading "(error on stderr…)" as covering the no-args case too is a fair reading. Check 4 only asks that lint is unchanged. Check 5 asks for the seven node:test cases and a README covering several files and the - argument. That is a fair reading of "documents the usage". Check 6 matches its line word for word. The stricter items (exit 2 winning over 1, nothing on stdout when - is given twice, stderr wording) are all under Advisory. None of the conditions requires mutation tests, branch rules or exact wording.
